title: Setting SMART goals for the crew
moduleTitle: Shared: Growing and managing a team
audience: Team leaders who want the crew to hit weekly or per-job targets and need goals that can be checked.
learningOutcomes: Rewrite a vague crew goal into a SMART goal with a measure and a deadline.
Break a crew goal into milestones with a named owner for each.
Check whether a goal fits the business's values before it is set.

instruction.heading: Why goals need structure
instruction.body: Distractions are constant on a cleaning crew. Urgent phone calls, a damaged item at a client's door, and a missing consumable can push the planned work aside. A goal written with enough detail gives the lead a map to return to. Without one, the crew works hard and still drifts away from what the business needs.

instruction.heading: The SMART test
instruction.body: A goal should be specific, meaning it describes what success looks like on the job. It should be measurable, with a number or a checklist score that shows progress. It should be attainable, which means a stretch is fine but not an impossible one. It should be realistic about the time, materials and people available. It should be timed, with a deadline for the final result and for the milestones along the way. Test each goal against all five words before you publish it.

instruction.heading: Milestones, owners and values
instruction.body: Split each goal into milestones that can be checked within a shift or a week. Give every milestone one owner, so there is no doubt about who reports on it. Finally, compare the goal with the business's stated values. A goal that rewards speed by sacrificing the client's trust does not fit the business, even if it looks good on a chart.

procedure: Write the crew goal in one sentence, then rewrite it so it names the result, the measure and the deadline.
Check the goal against each SMART word and change anything that fails.
Break the goal into two to four milestones, each with a date and an owner.
Compare the goal with the business's values and note any conflict.
Post the goal and milestones where the crew can see them, and review them at each shift handover.
Close the goal, record the result and set the next goal from what you learned.

workedExamples.situation: A short-stay turnover crew is told to 'do better on room turnaround'. The lead has no measure and no deadline.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How should the lead rewrite the goal, and what milestone would show early progress?
workedExamples.reasoning: A stronger version names the rooms, the agreed turnaround window, the checklist score and a four-week date. A milestone could be the first week's checklist results on a named set of rooms, owned by a named lead. The lead also checks that speed does not override the cleaning standard.

equipmentAndPpe: A whiteboard or shared sheet for the goal and milestones. Use the site's standard PPE on jobs.

commonErrors.error: Writing a goal with no number, so nobody can tell whether it was met.
commonErrors.prevention: Attach a measure such as a checklist score or a count of completed rooms.

commonErrors.error: Setting a stretch goal with no resources or time to reach it.
commonErrors.prevention: Check time, materials and people before publishing the goal.

commonErrors.error: Letting urgent problems replace the goal without a note.
commonErrors.prevention: Record any change to a goal and the reason for it.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Goals must not push workers to skip safety steps, rest breaks or site rules. Any target that does this must be changed.

qualityStandard: Each crew goal has a measure, a deadline and at least two dated milestones with named owners.
The goal has been checked against the business's stated values and any conflict is recorded.
documentationEvidence: Written goal with the SMART check completed.
Milestone record with owner, date and status.
summary: A SMART goal is specific, quantifiable, reachable, grounded in real resources and bounded by dates.
Milestones give early warning and each one needs one owner.
Goals that harm the standard, safety or values need changing, not just pushing harder.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which goal is written in the SMART form?
options: Improve the cleaning by working faster on every room and keep the rooms looking good for the client
Make the crew better this month and show it to the manager at the end of the month
Score at least 95 percent on the room checklist for all rooms by the end of next month
Work harder on every job and be faster than the other crews in the city every week

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the main purpose of a milestone?
options: To replace the final deadline and to close the job early for the client
To record the crew's pay and the hours they worked each week today
To make an owner unnecessary and to hand the whole job to a new lead today
To show early progress and let the lead correct course before the deadline

knowledgeChecks.question: A crew goal would reward finishing faster by skipping checks. What should the lead do?
options: Change the goal so speed does not override the standard and record the reason
Keep the goal because it is measurable and the crew likes the target
Hide the checks from the client and skip the checklist for the day
Remove all deadlines so the crew can take its time and let the job drag on
